entries.old: Elena pulls up the nav display. It's empty. No mapped systems, no trade routes, no faction boundaries. Just raw sensor data painting an unknown sky. But the yellow star ahead is stable. Three planets in the habitable zone. And the sensors are picking up structures, artificial, orbital, cold. Someone was here before us. Someone built something and left. She turns to you. Captain. We made it. We're somewhere no one in the Expanse has ever been. Her hand trembles on the console. What do we do now?

Priya is already moving, pulling up the Convergence schematics on her terminal. She speaks without looking up. The array positioning data includes spatial coordinates, reference points for the gravitational field calculations. I can invert the model. Instead of collapsing space, we use it to navigate. Give me ninety seconds. Her fingers blur across the console. Seventy-eight seconds later, she looks up. I have a stable exit point. A star system, outside the Expanse. A child's voice rises above the rest, asking a question you can't quite make out. The signal is a fragment of an old Earth broadcast, stretched across light-years and bent by gravity into something that sounds like a memory you never had.

entries.old: Hours of scanning reveal layers of complexity. The map includes eleven systems matching the known Expanse, and seven more beyond its borders, in regions no human vessel has reached. Isotope dating of the alloy returns contradictory results: some readings suggest thousands of years, others merely centuries. The engravings themselves show no tool marks your instruments can identify. The disc is either impossibly old or impossibly precise. Your data will keep scientists arguing for decades. You store the analysis alongside a single note in your log: 'We are not the first to find this place interesting.'

Drawings by children. Photographs printed on polymer sheets. A pressed flower, impossibly fragile, that disintegrates when the vacuum touches it. One letter, written in a steady hand, catches your eye: 'We are sending you everything we couldn't carry. Not cargo. Memory. Remember rain. Remember birdsong. Remember that the sky was blue. Build something worthy of what we lost.' You seal the container and store it with more care than anything else in your hold.

entries.old: Refurbished electronics stacked behind a vendor's counter  -- origin unknown, quality decent.

Wrecker's Outpost doesn't look like much from the airlock  -- welded hull plates, exposed conduit, a hand-painted sign reading WELCOME in six languages. But the air recyclers work, and nobody asks your name.
Loose deck plating shifts and rings underfoot  -- mismatched panels from salvaged freighters, not quite flush. Each step announces itself to the corridor.
Ore sample crates stamped with Union quality seals. Grade-A refined ore  -- someone's been skimming the yield reports.

The main gallery opens into a cathedral of carved rock. Heavy drilling rigs sit idle between shifts, ventilation fans humming where the machinery should roar. Thousands of tons of ore have passed through here  -- Breakstone's lifeblood, cut from the asteroid one blast at a time.
Something shifts in the darkness ahead. A faint light  -- chemical, not electric  -- flickers beyond a sealed door. Someone lives down here by choice. Someone who doesn't want to be found.
A sealed container with a cracked environmental seal. Rare metal alloys machined to specifications you've never seen  -- curved panels designed to focus energy along precise trajectories.

entries.old: An engineering workstation with data crystals scattered across it. Partial schematics glow on a dormant screen  -- concentric ring structures with gravitational field calculations in the margins.

The mining tunnel narrows as you descend past the marked depth levels. The rock changes color here  -- darker, denser. A sealed blast door ahead has been retrofitted with a modern access panel. Someone has been maintaining infrastructure that officially doesn't exist.

Beyond the blast door, everything changes. Rough-hewn rock gives way to fabricated walls  -- clean alloy panels, recessed lighting, atmospheric scrubbers humming at frequencies you associate with orbital stations, not mining tunnels. This is no storage depot. This is a manufacturing floor.

entries.old: The main corridor stretches the width of the facility. Through reinforced windows, you see assembly bays where curved metal panels are being shaped by automated presses. The scale is staggering  -- whatever they're building requires components measured in meters, not centimeters.

A research bay lined with holographic displays. Most are powered down, but one still cycles through structural simulations  -- concentric rings focusing energy inward toward a central point. The math scrolling alongside is beyond your training, but the diagram looks like a lens. A very large lens.

entries.old: The cargo lift at the facility's heart descends into darkness. Crate after crate lines the walls  -- all stamped with Commerce Guild freight codes, all addressed to recipients that don't appear in any public registry. The shipping dates span eighteen months. This operation has been running for longer than anyone suspected.
Maintenance supply crates  -- hull sealant, wiring harnesses, replacement filters. Everything brand new. This base is well-funded.
A personal locker, left unlocked. Credits, a worn star chart, a letter half-written and never sent. Even pirates have someone waiting somewhere.

entries.old: Data drives stacked in shielded cases. Financial records, patrol schedules, communications logs  -- encrypted, but Priya could crack these in her sleep.

The maintenance port is dark and cold  -- emergency lighting only, the air stale from minimal life support. Tomas checks his sidearm and grins. 'Unused maintenance port, they said. Nobody watches it, they said. Let's prove them right.'

The deck plates vibrate underfoot  -- a deep, steady pulse from generators buried in the asteroid's core. Someone spent a fortune building this place. Power generation, atmosphere processing, communications arrays. This isn't a hideout. It's an installation.

Holo-projectors line the walls. Star charts showing every system in the Expanse, shipping lanes marked in red, patrol routes highlighted with timestamps. And there  -- in the center of the command table  -- a network map. Lines connecting this base to nodes across the sector. Each labeled with a code name. This is The Ledger's command structure, laid bare.

The maintenance port groans as you pressurize the airlock. Colonial-era construction  -- riveted plates, manual overrides, emergency signage in a language standard that hasn't been used in decades. But the power conduits running along the ceiling are new. Military grade. Enough energy to power a small city.

The deck plates vibrate with a deep, steady pulse from generators buried in the station's core. Through a viewport in the service corridor, you see it for the first time  -- gravitational lensing arrays, sixteen of them, hanging in zero-gravity assembly cradles. Each one is enormous. Each one is nearly complete.

Crew quarters with military precision. A duty roster lists rotating shifts for 'Convergence Assembly Teams.' Status boards track array completion percentages  -- fourteen of sixteen read 100%. The last two show 94% and 97%. Days. Maybe hours.

The corridor narrows beyond reinforced blast doors, amber warning lights pulsing. A console on the wall displays real-time telemetry  -- energy readings from the Aurelia star, gravitational field calculations, array positioning data. Everything is green. The system is ready. They're just waiting for the order.

The command center opens into the assembly core's upper platform. Below, the arrays gleam under floodlights. But your eyes are drawn to the far wall  -- a warp gate frame, thirty meters across, already powered. Blue light pulses along its edges. This is the Ledger's escape route. When the star collapses, they walk through this gate and leave the Expanse behind. It's the only way out. And right now, it's yours.

entries.old: Arrived at Breakstone. Rock dust on everything  -- the handrails, the meal trays, the inside of your lungs if you stay long enough. The station thrums with a rhythm that never stops: drilling, hauling, drilling again. Someone's chalked a name and two dates on the corridor wall near Bay 3. Nobody's erased it.

Arrived at Crimson Reach. Dim lighting, exposed pipes, and the smell of coolant and old decisions. Half the overhead panels are dark. The other half flicker on a schedule nobody posted. A woman at the bar watched me dock through a porthole and looked away when I noticed. No questions asked here. That's not hospitality  -- it's policy.

That's the most unsettling thing about this place.

Word travels fast in mining towns. The shipyard owner knows about the investigation, and he's burning files, reassigning witnesses, and making threats that don't sound like threats until you think about them later.
